---
title: "Stochastic Compliance Minimization with Trace Estimation"
toc: true
---

## Description

When a load follows a distribution (magnitude, direction, or location), a
single deterministic compliance value no longer captures the structure's
performance. TopOpt.jl provides differentiable functions that average
compliance over many load scenarios, plus randomized estimators that
approximate the average without solving every scenario.

The methods used here — exact and randomized evaluation of the mean compliance,
of any scalar-valued function of the per-scenario compliances (e.g. a weighted
sum of the mean and standard deviation), and the augmented-Lagrangian handling
of a maximum-compliance constraint — are described in
[TarekRay2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.04594) and its approximate counterpart
[TarekRay2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.03654).

This tutorial covers:

- `MultiLoad` and `generate_scenarios` for building load ensembles
- `MeanComplianceFun` with the exact, SVD, Hutchinson-trace, and
  SVD-trace estimators
- `BlockComplianceFun` for per-scenario compliance, used in a risk-averse
  (mean + standard deviation) objective and in a maximum-compliance-constrained
  problem solved with the augmented Lagrangian method
- Choosing an estimator based on accuracy vs. cost

## Setup

```{julia}
#| output: false
using TopOpt, LinearAlgebra, SparseArrays, Random, Statistics
using WGLMakie
WGLMakie.activate!(; resize_to=:parent)
using Bonito
if haskey(ENV, "QUARTO_PROJECT_DIR")
    Bonito.Page(exportable=true, offline=true)
else
    Bonito.browser_display()
end
display_app(app) = display(app)
```

`WGLMakie.activate!(; resize_to=:parent)` selects the browser renderer and fills the Quarto output column. `Bonito.Page(exportable=true, offline=true)` embeds the assets needed by `visualize(...; static=true)` in the Quarto output, so the visualization does not require a running Julia process.

## A load ensemble

We model a cantilever whose tip is loaded by many random point loads drawn
from a distribution of directions and magnitudes. The load matrix `F` has one
column per scenario.

```{julia}
#| output: false
Random.seed!(42)
E, ν = 1.0, 0.3
nels = (40, 20)
base = PointLoadCantilever(nels, (1.0, 1.0), E, ν, 1.0)
ndofs = length(FEASolver(DirectSolver, base).u)
nloads = 16

F = spzeros(ndofs, nloads)
surface_dofs = vec(TopOpt.TopOptProblems.get_surface_dofs(base))
for i in 1:nloads
    dofs = surface_dofs[rand(1:length(surface_dofs), 2)]
    F[dofs, i] .= randn(2)
end
problem = MultiLoad(base, F)

solver = FEASolver(DirectSolver, problem; xmin=0.01, penalty=PowerPenaltyFun(2.0))
```

`generate_scenarios` builds a simpler ensemble: a single DOF loaded with
perturbed magnitudes.

```{julia}
#| output: true
F_simple = generate_scenarios(surface_dofs[1], (ndofs, 8), 1.0)
println("generate_scenarios: $(size(F_simple, 2)) scenarios, $(nnz(F_simple)) non-zeros")
```

## Exact mean compliance (baseline)

`MeanComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:exact)` solves every scenario and
averages. The `:exact_svd` method compresses `F` with a thin SVD first, giving
the same value from fewer solves when the scenarios are linearly dependent.

```{julia}
#| output: true
mc_exact = MeanComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:exact)
mc_svd   = MeanComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:exact_svd)

x = fill(0.5, length(solver.vars))
C_exact = mc_exact(PseudoDensities(x))
C_svd   = mc_svd(PseudoDensities(x))
println("exact     = $(C_exact)")
println("exact_svd = $(C_svd)  (rel. diff $(abs(C_exact - C_svd) / C_exact))")
```

## Hutchinson trace estimator

Instead of solving all `nloads` scenarios, the Hutchinson estimator probes with
`nv` random Rademacher (±1) vectors:

$$
\mathbb{E}\,[v^\mathsf{T} F^\mathsf{T} K^{-1} F v] = \mathrm{tr}(F^\mathsf{T} K^{-1} F)
$$

which is proportional to the mean compliance. `nv` is the number of probe
vectors; the estimate converges at `O(1/√nv)` but costs only `nv` solves.

```{julia}
#| output: true
for nv in (2, 4, 8, 16)
    mc = MeanComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:trace, nv=nv, sample_once=false)
    est = mc(PseudoDensities(x))
    println("hutch nv=$(lpad(nv, 2)): $(round(est, digits=3))  (rel. err $(round(abs(est - C_exact) / C_exact, digits=3)))")
end
```

With `sample_once=false` the probe vectors are redrawn on every call, so the
estimate varies between calls; with `sample_once=true` (the default) they are
drawn once at construction and held fixed, which keeps the objective and its
gradient consistent during an optimization.

## Hadamard (deterministic) estimator

Passing `sample_method=:hadamard` replaces the random probes with deterministic
orthogonal Hadamard columns. This removes the sampling noise and converges
smoothly, at the cost of a fixed `nv` that is a power of two.

```{julia}
#| output: true
for nv in (4, 8, 16)
    mc = MeanComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:trace, nv=nv, sample_method=:hadamard)
    est = mc(PseudoDensities(x))
    println("hadamard nv=$(lpad(nv, 2)): $(round(est, digits=3))  (rel. err $(round(abs(est - C_exact) / C_exact, digits=3)))")
end
```

## Per-scenario compliance: mean and standard deviation

`BlockComplianceFun` returns a vector of compliance values, one per scenario.
This lets us form arbitrary statistics. Minimizing the mean alone is the
standard robust formulation; adding a multiple of the standard deviation
penalizes designs that perform unevenly across the load distribution.

```{julia}
#| output: false
bc = BlockComplianceFun(problem, solver; method=:exact)
V = 0.5
filter = DensityFilterFun(solver; rmin=2.0)
volfrac = VolumeFun(solver)

mean_only = x -> mean(bc(filter(PseudoDensities(x))))
mean_std  = x -> mean(bc(filter(PseudoDensities(x)))) + 0.25 * std(bc(filter(PseudoDensities(x))))
volconstr = x -> volfrac(filter(PseudoDensities(x))) - V

function run(obj, label)
    model = Model(obj)
    addvar!(model, zeros(length(x)), ones(length(x)))
    add_ineq_constraint!(model, volconstr)
    r = optimize(model, MMA87(), fill(V, length(x));
        options=MMAOptions(; maxiter=100, tol=Tolerance(; kkt=1e-4, f=1e-4)))
    println("$label: obj = $(round(obj(r.minimizer), digits=3)), vol = $(round(volconstr(r.minimizer) + V, digits=3))")
    return r.minimizer
end
```

```{julia}
#| output: true
x_mean = run(mean_only, "mean only      ")
x_meanstd = run(mean_std, "mean + 0.25 std")
```

## Maximum compliance constraint via augmented Lagrangian

A robust design can instead bound the *worst-case* compliance: minimize the
volume subject to `C_i ≤ C_t` for every scenario. Following
[TarekRay2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.04594) (§4), this is solved with the
augmented Lagrangian method, where the per-scenario compliances from
`BlockComplianceFun` enter the augmented Lagrangian function

$$
L(\bm{x}; \bm\lambda, r) = V(\bm{x}) + \sum_i \left[\lambda_i (C_i - C_t) + r\,\max(C_i - C_t, 0)^2\right].
$$

Each subproblem minimizes this function over the box `0 ≤ x ≤ 1`, then the
multipliers and penalty are updated (`λ ← λ + ρ·c`, `ρ ← γρ`). The compliance
threshold `C_t` is calibrated from the solid design's worst-case compliance.

```{julia}
#| output: false
volf = x -> volfrac(filter(PseudoDensities(x)))
Cfun = x -> bc(filter(PseudoDensities(x)))
C_t = 2.0 * maximum(Cfun(ones(length(solver.vars))))

function al_subproblem(λ, ρ, x0)
    model = Model(xx -> begin
        C = Cfun(xx)
        c = C .- C_t
        pen = max.(λ .+ ρ .* c, 0.0)
        volf(xx) + (1 / (2ρ)) * (dot(pen, pen) - dot(λ, λ))
    end)
    addvar!(model, zeros(length(x0)), ones(length(x0)))
    return optimize(model, MMA87(), x0;
        options=MMAOptions(; maxiter=60, tol=Tolerance(; kkt=1e-4, f=1e-4))).minimizer
end
```

```{julia}
#| output: true
λ = zeros(nloads)
ρ = 1.0
x_al = ones(length(solver.vars))
for k in 1:20
    global λ, ρ, x_al
    x_al = al_subproblem(λ, ρ, x_al)
    C = Cfun(x_al)
    λ .= max.(λ .+ ρ .* (C .- C_t), 0.0)
    ρ *= 1.5
end
C = Cfun(x_al)
println("max-compliance design: volume = $(round(volf(x_al), digits=3)), max C = $(round(maximum(C), digits=1)), C_t = $(round(C_t, digits=1))")
```

`NonconvexPercival` provides this augmented-Lagrangian method as a built-in
solver. The same problem can be posed directly with a vector constraint and
solved by `PercivalAlg` (no manual multiplier loop):

```{julia}
#| eval: false
model = Model(volf)
addvar!(model, zeros(length(solver.vars)), ones(length(solver.vars)))
add_ineq_constraint!(model, x -> Cfun(x) ./ C_t .- 1)
x_al2 = optimize(model, PercivalAlg(), x_al;
    options=PercivalOptions(; max_iter=40, subsolver_max_eval=500)).minimizer
```

## Visualize the designs

```{julia}
#| label: fig-stochastic-mean
#| fig-cap: "Robust design minimizing mean compliance over random tip loads"
fig1 = visualize(problem.problem; static=true, topology=filter(PseudoDensities(x_mean)).x)
display_app(fig1)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-stochastic-meanstd
#| fig-cap: "Design minimizing mean + 0.25·std, trading a bit of average stiffness for consistency across the load distribution"
fig2 = visualize(problem.problem; static=true, topology=filter(PseudoDensities(x_meanstd)).x)
display_app(fig2)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-stochastic-al
#| fig-cap: "Minimum-volume design subject to a maximum-compliance bound (augmented Lagrangian)"
fig3 = visualize(problem.problem; static=true, topology=filter(PseudoDensities(x_al)).x)
display_app(fig3)
```

## Practical guidance

- **Exact** (`:exact`, `:exact_svd`): use when the number of scenarios is small
  (≤ a few dozen) or the scenarios are strongly correlated. `:exact_svd` is
  the better default — it gives the same answer with fewer solves.
- **Hutchinson** (`:trace`): use for large ensembles where solving every
  scenario is prohibitive. Accuracy improves with `nv`, but so does cost.
- **Hadamard** (`:trace` with `sample_method=:hadamard`): deterministic and
  smoother than Hutchinson; pick `nv` a power of two.
- `BlockComplianceFun` exposes the per-scenario values, so it is the tool for
  statistics beyond the mean (standard deviation, CVaR-style combinations) and
  for the maximum-compliance constraint handled by the augmented Lagrangian
  method.

- [TarekRay2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.03654): Tarek, M. & Ray, T.
